newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukrainians urged to invest privatisation vouchers.
newsitem.headline: Ukrainians urged to invest privatisation vouchers.

text.p: Ukraine, criticised for its slow pace of privatisation, is prodding its citizens to invest personal vouchers in thousands of state enterprises, a government adviser said on Tuesday.
"The emphasis in the next few months will be on investing the certificates," Myron Wasylyk, adviser to the State Property Fund (FDM), the state privatisation agency, told Reuters.
"We're focusing right now on making the availability of enterprises ample," he said.

If Ukraine reached its goal of privatising 5,000 enterprises by the end of the year, it would also receive a $100 million tranche of a $300 million enterprise and development loan from the World Bank, Wasylyk added.
While 82 percent of Ukrainians have collected the certificates, issued since January 1995, only about 20 million -- less than half the population -- have invested them.

The government, in an attempt to involve the whole country of 52 million people, has given every adult and child until December 31 to pick up a certificate worth about $280 each to buy shares in enterprises.

Ukraine intends to complete the planned sale of around 5,000 companies by the end of the year, and then to convert some 8,000 large- and medium-size enterprises into joint stock companies for potential share issues.
The government is expected to extend the investment deadline to the end of 1997 from the current mid-1997 deadline.
The Fund announced the latest batch of auctions of 403 medium and large enterprises on November 1.
"Experience in other countries shows that as privatisation comes to a close, investment through certificates rises exponentially," Wasylyk said.

However, investment companies have been buying the certificates from cash-strapped Ukrainians for $7 to $9 each, and emerging market fund specialist Caspian said last month it would raise $150 million to buy up the privatisation vouchers.
"It's perfectly legal, and 80 percent of certificates invested go through intermediaries," Wasylyk said.

Ukraine, which has attracted only about $1.5 billion in foreign investment since independence in 1991, has been criticised by international funding bodies and economic advisory groups for taking so long to privatise.

Wasylyk said 85 percent of the population was expected to collect vouchers by December 31 -- the third deadline set this year after many Ukrainians were scared off by the paperwork involved in acquiring a voucher.

"The pick-up deadline will remain December 31. At this point the position of the State Property Fund is that we are satisfied with the pick-up rate," Wasylyk said. "Eighty-five percent is perfectly normal and acceptable." --Irene Marushko, Kiev Newsroom +380 44 229 2264
